211.title: At-Takwir: the sun wrapped
211.hook: when the sun is folded up and the stars fall (81:1–2)
211.howItsDone: Many Muslims read At-Takwir together with Al-Infitar and Al-Inshiqaq as a picture of the Day of Resurrection, following a hadith that recommends them for that purpose; its opening is among the most widely memorized passages of the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Infitar, the sky cleaves, and a body created, fashioned and balanced. Your line was shaped in proportion. Did you look at your hands? Day two hundred eleven.

Think of the most reliable thing you know. Not a person, not a job. Something that has never once let you down. For almost everyone, it's the sun. It came up this morning. It came up on the day you were born and the day your grandparents were born. Every plan anyone has ever made assumes it. Now imagine a voice beginning: when the sun is folded up. The surah just before Al-Infitar starts exactly there, with the one thing nobody doubts, and then keeps going, a long list of whens. Today: At-Takwir, the sun wrapped.
screen: `THE MOST RELIABLE THING YOU KNOW.` → `WHEN THE SUN IS FOLDED UP.` → `AT-TAKWIR, THE SUN WRAPPED.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-one begins, in Pickthall's words: When the sun is overthrown, And when the stars fall. The Arabic verb is kuwwirat, from takwir, and it's a picture from everyday clothing. Kawwara is what you do with a turban: wind the cloth around and around, until it's wrapped up. So the sun, which spreads its light across everything, is wound up like cloth and put away. Then the list rolls on. The stars fall and dim. The mountains are moved. The camels ten months pregnant, the most precious thing a family in Arabia could own, are left untended, because nobody is thinking about wealth anymore. The wild animals are gathered. The seas are set alight. Twelve whens in all, and after them, one line: then a soul will know what it has brought. A hadith in Tirmidhi says that whoever wants to see the Day of Resurrection as if with their own eyes should read this surah, and Al-Infitar, and Al-Inshiqaq, the three we've just walked through. Another hadith in Tirmidhi reports that when Abu Bakr told the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ his hair had turned gray, he named a few surahs that had done it, and this was one. So why start with the sun? Because if even the sun can be wrapped and put away, then everything can. Every tower, every fortune, every plan. The Qur'an says it elsewhere in plain words: everyone upon the earth will pass away, and the face of your Lord remains. That isn't meant to make life feel pointless. It's meant to tell you where the one thing that lasts is.
screen: `KUWWIRAT — WOUND UP LIKE A TURBAN.` · `THE PRECIOUS CAMELS, LEFT UNTENDED.` · `TWELVE WHENS, THEN ONE SOUL.` · `IF EVEN THE SUN, THEN EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING ENDS BUT HIM.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, look at one thing near you that feels permanent: a wall, a table, a heavy old book. It was made, and one day it won't be here. Then bring to mind something heavier, a worry you've carried for months or a win you're proud of. Hold it lightly, the way you'd hold cloth you're about to fold and put away. Then notice what's still here: your breath, this moment, and the One Muslims say remains. The bell holds the time.
At-Takwir. The wrapping up, the sun wound like a turban, and the name of Surah eighty-one. Today's word.
Your line: everything ends but him. When something today feels permanent, a worry or a win, remember the sun can be wrapped, and let it sit a little lighter. Day two hundred eleven.

212.title: At-Takwir: the buried girl
212.hook: when the baby girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed (81:8–9)
212.howItsDone: Muslims read these verses as the Qur'an's condemnation of female infanticide; the hadith on raising daughters is often quoted at the birth of a girl, and many families celebrate a daughter's birth with an 'aqiqah, a sacrifice and a shared meal of thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Takwir, the sun wound up like a turban and put away. Your line was everything ends but him. Did something feel a little lighter? Day two hundred twelve.

Among the twelve whens of At-Takwir, the sun wrapped, the stars falling, the seas on fire, there is one that isn't about the sky at all. It's about a single child. Of everything the surah could have chosen to show on the last day, the biggest events in the universe, it stops for one small girl whom nobody in her own world stopped for. Today's lesson is a hard one, and it's told gently. It's about who gets to speak on that day, and who has to answer. Today: the buried girl.
screen: `THE SUN, THE STARS, THE SEAS.` → `AND ONE SMALL GIRL.` → `THE BURIED GIRL.`

segments.voice: Verses eight and nine, in Pickthall's words: "And when the girl-child that was buried alive is asked For what sin she was slain." In pre-Islamic Arabia, some tribes, not all, practiced the killing of newborn daughters. Fear of poverty, fear of shame if a daughter were captured in a raid, and a culture that counted sons as wealth. The Qur'an describes the reaction elsewhere: when one of them is told a daughter has been born, his face darkens, and he hides from people, wondering whether to keep her in humiliation or bury her in the dust. The Qur'an forbade it outright: do not kill your children for fear of poverty. Now look closely at how verse nine is built. The question isn't put to the father. It's put to her. For what sin was she killed? Commentators notice this. The one who had no voice in her short life is the one addressed on that day, in front of everyone, and her answer will be the testimony. And the question itself contains its answer: no sin. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ went further than forbidding. A hadith in Muslim's collection says that whoever raises two daughters until they grow up will come on the Day of Resurrection with him, and he held his fingers together to show how close. He had daughters himself, and was known for standing up to greet Fatima when she came into the room. So the surah names the harm, gives the girl the question, and the Prophet's practice turns the shame upside down: raising a daughter becomes a way to be close to him.
screen: `AL-MAW'UDAH — THE BURIED GIRL.` · `SOME TRIBES, NOT ALL.` · `THE QUESTION IS PUT TO HER.` · `RAISING DAUGHTERS, CLOSE TO HIM.` · then, large: `SHE WILL BE ASKED.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, bring to mind a girl or woman in your life. A daughter, a sister, a niece, a mother, a student, a friend. Picture her face. Think of one thing about her that deserves to be honored out loud: her courage, her humor, her work. Then decide how you'll tell her, today. If there's no one close, hold in mind girls anywhere whose lives aren't valued. The bell holds the time.
At-Takwir. The wrapping up, Surah eighty-one, where the buried girl is asked for what sin she was killed. Today's word.
Your line: she will be asked. Honor one girl or woman today, in words she can hear, for something real. Day two hundred twelve.

213.title: 'Abasa: he frowned
213.hook: the Prophet ﷺ turned from a blind man to talk to the powerful, and was corrected (80:1–10)
213.carry: turn to the one who came
213.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 'Abasa as a lesson that sincerity outweighs status; Ibn Umm Maktum is remembered as a companion and muezzin, and the surah is recited as part of the thirtieth part of the Qur'an that many memorize.

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Takwir, and the buried girl who is given the question. Your line was she will be asked. Did you honor one girl or woman in words she could hear? Day two hundred thirteen.

You're at a work event, finally talking to the one person in the room who could change everything. The investor, the boss's boss, the person with the answer. And someone taps your shoulder. It's the intern, or an old neighbor, asking a question that could wait. You don't say anything rude. Your face just does a small thing. A flicker. A frown. Most of us would never think about it again. The surah just before At-Takwir is named after that flicker. And the surprising part is whose face it was. Today: 'Abasa, he frowned.
screen: `FINALLY TALKING TO THE RIGHT PERSON.` → `A TAP ON THE SHOULDER.` → `'ABASA, HE FROWNED.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty opens, in Pickthall's words: He frowned and turned away Because the blind man came unto him. Sunni commentators, following reports in Tirmidhi and the tafsir, explain the scene this way. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was in Mecca, speaking with leaders of the Quraysh, hoping they would listen. A blind man, 'Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, came up asking to be taught. The Prophet frowned and turned back to the leaders. And revelation came correcting him. Many Shia commentators, and some others, read it differently: that the one who frowned was another man present, not the Prophet. Both readings are held with care. Now listen to how the correction is spoken. It begins in the third person, he frowned, almost as if the text is looking away out of courtesy. Then it turns and speaks directly: what could tell you, perhaps he would grow in purity, or be reminded, and the reminder would help him. As for the one who thinks he needs nothing, you give him your attention. But the one who came to you eagerly, and in awe, him you neglect. That's remarkable on its own: the Qur'an keeps a correction in its text, recited every day for fourteen centuries. And what happened next? Ibn Umm Maktum became one of the two men who gave the call to prayer in Medina, alongside Bilal, and reports say the Prophet left him in charge of the prayer in Medina when he traveled. The man turned away from became the voice calling the city to prayer.
screen: `HE FROWNED AND TURNED AWAY.` · `IBN UMM MAKTUM, WHO CAME TO LEARN.` · `A CORRECTION KEPT IN THE TEXT.` · `THE VOICE THAT CALLED MEDINA.` · then, large: `TURN TO THE ONE WHO CAME.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, think of the people who come to you and are easy to overlook. The quiet coworker, the kid who wants to show you something, the older relative who repeats a story, the person at the counter. Pick one. Picture the next time they come to you, and picture turning fully toward them: phone down, eyes up, full attention. The bell holds the time.
'Abasa. He frowned, the name of Surah eighty, which turns our attention to the one who came eagerly. Today's word.
Your line: turn to the one who came. Today, when someone easy to overlook comes to you, give them your full face, even for one minute. Day two hundred thirteen.

214.title: 'Abasa: look at your food
214.hook: let the human look at his food: rain, grain, grapes, olives, palms (80:24–32)
214.tomorrow: 'Abasa: the day a man flees his brother
214.howItsDone: Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after, eat with the right hand, and try not to waste food; these verses of 'Abasa are often recalled as a reminder that every meal begins with rain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'Abasa, he frowned, and the blind man who came eagerly. Your line was turn to the one who came. Who did you turn toward? Day two hundred fourteen.
screen: `'ABASA — TURN TO THE ONE WHO CAME.`

segments.voice: Think about your last meal. Where did it come from? The honest answer for most of us is: a store, a delivery bag, a drive-through window. Maybe a plastic tray with a sticker on it. The food shows up already finished, with the whole story cut off. Somewhere there was rain, and dirt, and a seed, and months of sun, and people bent over in a field. None of that is on the sticker. 'Abasa, after the story of the frown, turns to a very different subject, and asks us to do something almost nobody does anymore. Today: look at your food.
screen: `A TRAY WITH A STICKER.` → `THE STORY CUT OFF.` → `LOOK AT YOUR FOOD.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-four, in Pickthall's words: Let man consider his food. Look at it. Then the surah tells its story backward, from the plate to the sky. We pour water down in showers. Then We split the earth open, in clefts. Then We cause grain to grow in it, and grapes, and green fodder, and olive trees and date palms, and gardens thick with trees, and fruit, and grasses. Provision for you, and for your animals. Rain, cracked soil, a sprout, a harvest. It reads like a slow-motion film of a seed. And it lands on two words: for you, and for your cattle. The whole cycle is described as a gift, set down in front of you. One word in that list is famous for a different reason. The word for grasses, abb. A well-known report says that 'Umar, one of the closest companions, read this verse and admitted he didn't know exactly what abb meant, and then decided not to force a meaning onto it. Scholars today mostly say it means pasture, the plants that animals graze. But the honesty is worth keeping: even the first generation said, sometimes, we don't know exactly. Notice where this passage sits. Right after the surah reminds the human being he was made from a drop, and asks why he is ungrateful. The answer to ingratitude isn't a lecture. It's: look at your plate. Just look. Trace one bite back to the rain. That's also why many Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after. Two small words to bracket the story.
screen: `LET MAN CONSIDER HIS FOOD.` · `RAIN, CRACKED EARTH, GRAIN, FRUIT.` · `ABB — EVEN 'UMAR WASN'T SURE.` · `BISMILLAH BEFORE, ALHAMDULILLAH AFTER.` · then, large: `LOOK AT YOUR FOOD.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, choose one thing you ate today, or will eat soon. A piece of bread, an apple, rice. Trace it backward: the kitchen, the store, the truck, the field, the hands that picked it, the sun, the rain, the seed. Go as far back as you can. When you reach the rain, stop, and just hold it. The bell holds the time.
'Abasa. He frowned, Surah eighty, which also says: let the human look at his food, rain to grain to fruit. Today's word.
Your line: look at your food. At your next meal, before the first bite, look at it for five seconds and think of the rain. Day two hundred fourteen.

215.title: 'Abasa: the day a man flees his brother
215.hook: on that day each flees mother, father, wife and children (80:34–37)
215.howItsDone: Muslims read the end of 'Abasa as a description of the Day of Resurrection, and many take it as a reason to keep family ties, silat al-rahim, strong now, visiting parents and relatives and mending quarrels.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'Abasa, and a meal traced back to the rain. Your line was look at your food. Did you look before the first bite? Day two hundred fifteen.

Picture a crowded family photo. Grandparents in the middle, cousins squeezed in at the edges, someone's kid making a face. These are the people who would run into a burning building for you, and you for them. That's what family means: when the worst happens, you move toward each other. The end of 'Abasa describes a day when that instinct runs the other way. It's one of the most unsettling images in the Qur'an, and it isn't there to frighten for its own sake. It's there to say something about today, while the photo is still full. Today: the day a man flees his brother.
screen: `A CROWDED FAMILY PHOTO.` → `WHEN THE WORST HAPPENS, YOU MOVE TOWARD.` → `A DAY IT RUNS THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Verse thirty-three: when the deafening blast comes. The word is as-sakhkhah, a sound so loud it strikes the ears. Then verse thirty-four, in Pickthall's words: On the day when a man fleeth from his brother. And then the list goes on: and his mother and his father, and his wife and his children. Commentators notice the order. It moves inward, from a brother, to the parents who raised you, to the spouse beside you, to your own children, the closest of all. The circle of people you'd die for, one ring at a time, and each one fled. Why? Verse thirty-seven: every one of them, that day, will have concern enough of his own. Not cruelty. Overwhelm. Each person standing alone with their own record, the way we heard in At-Takwir: a soul will know what it has brought. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim adds a human moment. Aisha heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ describe people raised on that day, and she asked, wouldn't they look at one another? He answered that the matter would be too serious for that, and recited this verse. Then the surah ends with faces again, the way Al-Ghashiyah did. Some faces that day bright, laughing, rejoicing. Some covered in dust. So what is this for? Not to make you afraid of your family. It's the opposite. That day, each is alone. Today, you are not. Today the brother can still be called, the mother visited, the child held. The verse turns the present into something precious, because it won't always be like this.

segments.voice: For two minutes, picture the people closest to you, one ring at a time. A sibling or a friend like one. Your parents, or whoever raised you. A partner. Children, if you have them, or the young people you love. Let each face come clearly. Today they are all within reach. Choose one to hold close today: a call, a visit, a long hug. The bell holds the time.
'Abasa. He frowned, Surah eighty, which ends with a day when each person flees even the people closest to them. Today's word.
Your line: each alone that day. So today, while you can, hold someone close, and tell them something you'd regret not saying. Day two hundred fifteen.

216.title: An-Nazi'at: those who pull out
216.hook: by the angels who draw out souls gently and harshly (79:1–2)
216.howItsDone: Muslims believe angels take each soul at death; many pray for an easy passing, and at a deathbed family often recite the shahada gently and read Qur'an, hoping the soul is drawn out with ease.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of 'Abasa, a day when each person flees even their own family. Your line was each alone that day. Who did you hold close? Day two hundred sixteen.

If you've ever sat with someone at the end of their life, you may remember the breathing most. Long pauses. The room holding still. And then the moment when a breath goes out and doesn't come back in. People who've been there often say it was quieter than they expected, and sometimes, strangely, peaceful. Every tradition has had to find words for that moment. The surah just before 'Abasa opens with its own words for it, in a pair of oaths that are hard to translate and have been read several ways. Today: An-Nazi'at, those who pull out.
screen: `THE LAST BREATH IN A QUIET ROOM.` → `QUIETER THAN EXPECTED.` → `AN-NAZI'AT, THOSE WHO PULL OUT.`

segments.voice: Surah seventy-nine begins with an oath: by those who pull out, forcefully. Then: by those who draw out, gently. The first word, an-nazi'at, is from a root meaning to pull, to wrench something out. The second, an-nashitat, has a softer picture behind it: loosening a knot, or easing a bucket up out of a well. The surah doesn't say who these are. Most commentators say they are angels, the ones who take souls at death. From some, the soul is pulled out hard. From others, it is drawn out gently. Other early commentators read the oaths as stars moving across the sky, or as death itself, or as arrows drawn from a bow. The text leaves it open, and the scholars have left it open too. But the angels reading is the one most Muslims know, and a long hadith, reported in Abu Dawud and in Ahmad's collection, fills it in. It says that when a believer dies, the soul leaves as easily as a drop of water flows from the mouth of a waterskin. And for others, it is dragged like a skewer through wet wool. Hard to hear. But notice that the surah doesn't stop at the hard picture. The very next oath is gently. Many Muslims pray for exactly this, an easy departure, and ask at the bedsides of the dying for the soul to be drawn out gently. And in this reading, death isn't a stranger crashing in. It's a door that's attended to. Someone is sent. Someone does the drawing out. As Muslims read these verses, nobody leaves unaccompanied.
screen: `AN-NAZI'AT — PULLED OUT HARD.` · `AN-NASHITAT — A KNOT LOOSENED.` · `ANGELS, STARS, OR DEATH ITSELF.` · `NOBODY LEAVES UNACCOMPANIED.` · then, large: `GENTLY DRAWN.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, just watch your breath going out. Not in. Out. Let each exhale be slow and complete, like water poured from a jug until it's empty. Notice the small pause at the bottom before the next breath comes on its own. Nothing to fix. Just the out-breath, gently drawn, and the one that comes after. The bell holds the time.
An-Nazi'at. Those who pull out, the opening word of Surah seventy-nine, paired with those who draw out gently. Today's word.
Your line: gently drawn. Once today, when you're tense, let one long breath out, slowly, all the way to the bottom. Day two hundred sixteen.

reported in Abu Dawud and in Ahmad's Musnad.

fork.setup: An-Nazi'at swears by 'those who pull out' and 'those who draw out gently'. who do most commentators say they are?
fork.reveal: most say the angels who take souls at death; others read stars, death itself, or arrows. the text leaves it open.

original.note: Arabic: "those who pull out," from n-z-', to pull or wrench out; the name of Surah 79.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah that starts with something scary.
what it means: oaths by those who draw souls out, some hard, some gently, read by most as the angels at death.

what a scholar hears: gharqan, drowning deep, qualifies the first oath; the angels reading goes back to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas in al-Tabari; the waterskin image is from the long hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.

sources.ref: Qur'an 79:1–5 (those who pull out, those who draw out gently, those who glide, race, and arrange)
Sunan Abi Dawud 4753; Musnad Ahmad (the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib on the soul's departure)
al-Tabari on 79:1–2 (angels, stars, death, arrows)

217.title: An-Nazi'at: Musa, again
217.hook: go to Pharaoh, he has transgressed, and ask, would you purify yourself (79:17–19)
217.howItsDone: Musa is one of the prophets most often mentioned in the Qur'an; Muslims read his mission to Pharaoh as a model of calling others with gentle speech, following the instruction in Ta-Ha to speak to him gently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: An-Nazi'at, and souls drawn out, some hard, some gently. Your line was gently drawn. Did you let one long breath out, all the way? Day two hundred seventeen.

Think of the hardest person you've ever had to talk to. The boss who humiliates people in meetings. The relative who only hears himself. Now imagine being sent to him with a message he won't want. Most of us would rehearse either a speech or a fight. The Qur'an tells the story of Musa, Moses, many times, and early on this path we followed him for two weeks, as far as the fire in the valley of Tuwa. In An-Nazi'at he comes back, briefly, and he's sent to one of the hardest listeners in the whole Qur'an: Pharaoh, a king who calls himself a god. What's surprising is the first thing Musa is told to say. It isn't a threat. It's a question. Today: Musa, again.
screen: `THE HARDEST PERSON TO TALK TO.` → `A KING WHO CALLS HIMSELF A GOD.` → `MUSA, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Verse fifteen asks: has the story of Musa reached you? His Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa. Go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed. And say to him, verse eighteen: would you like to purify yourself? And I will guide you to your Lord, so you'll hold Him in awe. That's the whole opening. An invitation, in the form of a question, to the most arrogant ruler in the story. The verb is tazakka, from z-k-y. We've met it twice already on this stretch: in Ash-Shams, successful is the one who purifies the soul, and in Al-A'la, successful is the one who purifies himself. Now the same word is offered to Pharaoh himself. Even he is invited to the thing that makes a soul succeed. Elsewhere, in Surah Ta-Ha, Musa and his brother Harun are told the same thing in other words: speak to him gently, perhaps he will remember or fear. Then Musa shows him the great sign. Pharaoh denies, turns away, gathers his people, and proclaims: I am your lord, the most high. Al-a'la, the very word from the surah we read two weeks ago. A man claiming the title of the Most High. And he is seized. The surah ends the story: in this is a lesson for whoever holds God in awe. It's the end of a week, too. The sun wrapped and the buried girl given her question. The frown, the food, the day each person flees. Souls gently drawn. And now a question offered to a tyrant. Nobody, the surah suggests, is beyond being asked.
screen: `THE SACRED VALLEY OF TUWA.` · `A QUESTION, NOT A THREAT.` · `TAZAKKA — OFFERED EVEN TO PHARAOH.` · `I AM YOUR LORD THE MOST HIGH.` · then, large: `WOULD YOU PURIFY YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, think of someone you find hard to talk to. Not the worst person in the world. Just someone where every conversation goes badly. Picture opening the next one with a gentle question instead of a point. Not a trick. A real question, like: what would help? How are you, really? Choose the words. The bell holds the time.
An-Nazi'at. Those who pull out, Surah seventy-nine, where Musa is sent to Pharaoh with a question. Today's word.
Your line: would you purify yourself. Offer one gentle question today to someone you'd rather argue with, and listen to the answer. Day two hundred seventeen.

myth: Musa is told to begin with a threat of punishment
he's told to begin with a question: would you purify yourself?
tazakka also appears in Ash-Shams and Al-A'la
the same root z-k-y: to purify and to grow.
Pharaoh in this surah calls himself the most high
ana rabbukum al-a'la (79:24), the word that names Surah 87.

fork.setup: you are Musa, sent to a king who calls himself a god. what are you told to say first?
fork.reveal: would you purify yourself, and I will guide you to your Lord (79:18–19). the tyrant is offered the same success as anyone.

original.note: Arabic: "purify yourself," from z-k-y, the root of zakat, offered to Pharaoh in 79:18.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses confronts Pharaoh.
what it means: Musa's first words to the tyrant are an invitation: would you purify yourself, and let me guide you to your Lord?
what a scholar hears: hal laka ila an tazakka is phrased with great courtesy, like would you care to; Tuwa appears also in 20:12; Pharaoh's rabbukum al-a'la in 79:24 echoes al-a'la of 87:1.

sources.ref: Qur'an 79:15–26 (Musa at Tuwa; would you purify yourself; I am your lord the most high; a lesson for whoever fears)
Qur'an 20:12, 20:43–44 (Tuwa; speak to him gently)
Qur'an 91:9; 87:14 (the same root, tazkiyah)
